# Links

The guaranteed interoperability vocabulary is generated from the engine contract:

- `relates_to`
- `implements`
- `depends_on`
- `blocks`
- `supersedes`
- `owned_by`
- `member_of`
- `part_of`
- `derived_from`

`manage_links.relationship` remains open-additive as a compatibility surface. Its generic graph links are stored as sealed, directed `legacy_link.v1` relationship assertions; even `relates_to` remains directional here, so A→B and B→A are distinct. Prefer the guaranteed terms when their meaning fits so shared clients and skills can interoperate; use a novel relationship only when none is truthful. Message, federated-reference, and engine-semantic links remain content-owned.

### `relates_to`

A deliberately weak association when no stronger guaranteed relationship is true.

### `implements`

The source realizes or carries out the target specification, resolution, or requirement.

### `depends_on`

The source cannot complete correctly without the target.

### `blocks`

The source currently prevents the target from progressing. This is directional and is not automatically inferred from `depends_on`.

### `supersedes`

The source replaces the target while preserving an explicit historical trail.

### `owned_by`

The source is accountable to the target entity or ownership record. This link can add context beyond the first-class owner facet.

### `member_of`

The source participates in the target group or collection without implying containment.

### `part_of`

The source is a constituent of the target whole. It is semantic composition, not the canonical browse home.

### `derived_from`

The source was produced from the target and should retain that provenance.

Use `manage_links` for atomic add/remove/list operations. Use `query_record` traversal for filtered multi-hop work; traversing a link never changes containment.

Use `manage_relationships` for governed semantic propositions whose support,
contest, evidence, admission, provenance, and effective state must remain
explainable. Its v1 public types are `relates_to`, `depends_on`, `blocks`,
`assigned_to`, and `answerable_by`. The server derives endpoint metadata,
canonical identity, and admission evidence; these relationships never grant
View, Edit, or Manage access. `on_behalf_of` is optional semantic context on an
assertion, not verified delegation or authority.

`manage_relationships` reads are viewer-scoped. `read` and `why` explain one
relationship you can already name. `find` answers the other question — "what is
assigned to this person?" — from one endpoint, and is the only read that does
not require a relationship id.

`find` scopes at exactly one endpoint: `endpoint_record_id`, or
`endpoint_current_person: true` for the person bound to the calling credential.
From there it filters on `relationship_type`, `endpoint_role` (the role the
scoped record holds, i.e. direction), `effective_state`, `epistemic_state`, and
`counterpart_lifecycle`, so "open tasks assigned to me" is a single call.
Results are ordered by `occurred_at` descending with a stable coordinate
tiebreak, and paged with `limit` (default 25, maximum 200) and `offset`.

Each result carries the counterpart endpoint inline — role, record id, type,
kind, name and lifecycle — so rendering a feed needs no follow-up read per row.
It also carries BOTH reduction axes: `effective.state`
(`active`/`inactive`/`unresolved`/`retired`) and `effective.epistemic_state`
(`unsupported`/`supported`/`contested`/`incomplete`). "Assigned, and two parties
disagree" is a different fact from "assigned, uncontested"; never collapse the
two axes into one boolean.

Visibility is all-or-nothing and never partial. A relationship whose counterpart
you cannot View is absent from results — never returned with a nulled or
redacted field, because a redacted row would still disclose that it exists. That
filters which relationships you are shown; it never changes what the reducer
concluded about a shown one. An assertion issued from a record you cannot see
still makes a relationship read as `contested`. Because visibility is applied
per candidate row, a page can be shorter than `limit`; `scan_limit_reached`
tells you when the bounded candidate scan, rather than the end of the data, ended
the page.
